claims.claim: The American Psychological Association defines resilience as the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment.

Resilience is common and usually arises from the normative functions of ordinary human adaptational systems; the greatest threats to development are those that compromise these protective systems (Masten, 2001).
After loss or potentially traumatic events, many people show only minor and transient disruptions in functioning; resilience is a common response, not a rare one (Bonanno, 2004).

Good developmental outcomes occur even in suboptimal circumstances, and it takes extreme deprivation at specific developmental times to severely restrict a developing human's potential (OpenStax Lifespan Development).

Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood (ages 0-17) and include abuse and neglect, witnessing violence, and household challenges such as parental separation, a family member's mental health problems, substance use in the home, and household members being in jail or prison (CDC).
About 64 percent of U.S. adults report having experienced at least one type of ACE before age 18, and about 17 percent report four or more types (CDC page reviewed April 2024).

Factors that help people adapt to adversity include the availability and quality of social resources and specific coping strategies, and the resources and skills associated with resilience can be cultivated and practiced (APA).

Poverty is linked to added stress for children; the CDC notes that some children face toxic stress from historical and ongoing traumas, including the impacts of poverty on educational and economic opportunities.
Risk factors shift the odds of difficulty at the group level but do not determine any individual child's outcome; risk is odds, not destiny (synthesis of CDC, Masten, and OpenStax findings).

positions: Risk factors are sometimes read as predictions of a specific child's future
Research shows group-level odds do not translate into reliable individual predictions; most children in adverse conditions develop along typical paths
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames risk strictly as population-level odds and states explicitly that odds are not destiny; no individual predictions are offered anywhere in the lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is resilience a fixed trait or a developable process?
positions: Popular view: resilience is an inborn trait some children have and others lack
APA and developmental research treat resilience as a process and outcome that can be cultivated through resources and skills
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the process framing and cites APA; Masten's ordinary-magic finding reinforces that resilience is common rather than exceptional. The trait view is named in Common Mistakes as an error.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's vocabulary entry defined the topic circularly ('A foundational Human Development concept covered in this lesson') and carried no factual content.
The generated draft's Eli-10 toolbox-drawer analogy and generic 'context / evidence / application' vocabulary had no verifiable content about risk or resilience.
The generated draft contained no factual claims about risk factors, protective factors, or resilience research; all lesson content was written from verified sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generated-draft boilerplate with source-verified content.
Added the APA-attributed definition of resilience and a research-grounded definition of risk as raised odds.
Added CDC-verified risk-factor categories (poverty, illness, family stress, adversity), each stated factually without scare content.
Added protective-factor categories (caring adults, skills, community supports) with original examples (Lena, Marcus, Maya).
Attributed the ordinary-magic finding to Masten and the odds-not-destiny framing to the resilience literature; added the development-bends framing attributed to OpenStax's plasticity discussion.
rightsIssues: All five sources are reference-only; the lesson is original synthesis with short attributed paraphrases of definitions; no source wording is reproduced at length.
No reuse license is stated on the APA, CDC, or ERIC pages, and none is inferred from their domains.

sourceRecords.title: Resilience (Psychology Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the APA definition of resilience as the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, the role of social resources and coping strategies in how well people adapt to adversity, and the finding that resilience-related resources and skills can be cultivated and practiced. The live page blocked direct retrieval from this session, so it was read from an Internet Archive capture dated 2 January 2025 of the canonical URL. The definition is paraphrased with attribution in the lesson; no wording reproduced at length.

sourceRecords.title: About Adverse Childhood Experiences
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definition of adverse childhood experiences, the household-challenge categories (parental separation, family mental health problems, substance use, household members in jail or prison), the poverty-toxic-stress link, the statement that certain factors increase or decrease risk, and prevalence figures (64% of U.S. adults report at least one ACE; 17.3% report four or more). Read this session from an Internet Archive capture of the page carrying a CDC review date of 9 April 2024 (cdc.gov blocks direct fetch); the lesson does not present the figures as current-year statistics. No reuse license stated; none inferred.

sourceRecords.title: Ordinary Magic: Resilience Processes in Development (American Psychologist, 56(3), 227-238)
sourceRecords.provider: Masten, A. S. / American Psychological Association, indexed by ERIC (EJ627466)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the ordinary-magic finding: resilience is common and usually arises from the normative functions of human adaptational systems, the greatest threats to development are those that compromise protective systems, and the study of resilience overturned many negative assumptions about children growing up in adverse conditions. ERIC record and abstract re-verified directly this session; article text not retrieved and nothing reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 1.2: Themes of Development
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the plasticity framing: good outcomes occur even in suboptimal circumstances, resilience is the capacity to adapt well in the face of adversity (citing APA), and it takes extreme deprivation at specific developmental times to severely restrict a developing human's potential. OpenStax blocks direct fetch, so this session read an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL. OpenStax books are CC BY licensed, but the lesson adapts no textbook wording; facts are restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Loss, Trauma, and Human Resilience: Have We Underestimated the Human Capacity to Thrive After Aversive Events?
sourceRecords.provider: Bonanno, G. A. / American Psychological Association (American Psychologist, 59(1), 20-28)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the claim that many people exposed to loss or potentially traumatic events show only minor and transient disruptions in functioning, and that resilience is a common trajectory rather than a rare one. Verified through the registry record (abstract read via Europe PMC, PMID 14736317, checked 2026-08-18) and cited at title-level claim strength; full text not retrieved and nothing reproduced.
